    #73484. Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1143 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Whether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.
    • Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
    • Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Whether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.

    Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment. But rising Medicare premiums could chip away at the increase — and as beneficiaries' incomes rise, that may affect the taxes they owe and their eligibility for a newly introduced senior deduction.

    Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.

    Here's a breakdown of what to expect in the upcoming year.

    Social Security's limit for payroll taxes is adjusted every year to reflect the average wage index.

    It has been revealed that in 2027, the taxable maximum will go up to $192,300 in earnings, up from $184,500 in 2026. Workers and employers each pay a 6.2% payroll tax on earnings up to that limit — or 12.4% for self-employed workers. Medicare taxes of 1.45% for both workers and employers are not subject to a limit.

    In 2027, workers who earn $192,300 or more will pay $11,922.60 in total Social Security payroll taxes, according to the Social Security Administration, while self-employed workers will pay $23,845.20.

    "If you're somebody whose income is over what the new threshold is going to be, this increase in the threshold results in a tax increase to you," said Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird.

    The 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to increase retirement benefits by about $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration.

    Sources indicate that the annual adjustment is the largest boost to benefits since 2023 due to rising inflation. The COLA averaged 2.6% from 2000 to 2026, according to the Senior Citizens League, a nonpartisan senior group.

    Around 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see benefit increases, according to the agency.

    The maximum benefit for a worker at full retirement age — when individuals become eligible for 100% of the benefits they've earned — will rise to $4,188 per month in 2027, up from $4,152 per month in 2026, according to the federal agency. To be eligible for the maximum benefit at full retirement age — typically age 66 to 67 — you generally have to earn up to the taxable threshold for each of your working years factored into the calculation.

    How much of the COLA increase Social Security beneficiaries see depends in part on their Medicare premiums, which may be deducted directly from benefit checks.

    Monthly rates are poised to increase for both Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary services and preventive care, and Part D, which provides prescription drug coverage.

    The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 in 2027 — a $6.50 increase from $202.90 in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

    Industry observers note that "It's not often that we see a Part B [premium] increase that is lower than the COLA," Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, noted of the 3.2% increase. The last time that happened was in 2023, she said.

    Medicare Part D beneficiaries may also pay higher premiums in 2027.

    In a recent development, assuming enrollees keep the same plan, the average enrollment-weighted monthly Part D premium may be $51 in 2027, up 50% from $34 in 2026, according to projections from KFF, a provider of health policy research and polling. That is higher than CMS' projections, which forecast the national average premium for standalone Part D prepares will rise about $1, to $36, in 2027 from $35 in 2026.

    According to recent reports, standard monthly premiums for Part B and blueprint-specific premiums for Part D apply to individuals who have $112,000 or less in modified adjusted gross income, or $224,000 for married couples. Beneficiaries with higher income pay larger premiums because of income-related monthly adjustment amounts, which affect 9% of Medicare Part B and Part D beneficiaries, according to CMS.

    With bigger Social Security benefits, more households may find that some portion of benefits is taxable — though a new senior deduction may help provide some relief to those who are eligible.

    It has been revealed that social Security benefits may be subject to federal income taxes for certain individuals. The thresholds at which those taxes are applied are not adjusted from year to year.

    Whether or not benefits are taxed is determined by a formula known as combined income — the sum of adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest income and half of Social Security benefits:.

    Individuals who are subject to taxes may opt to withhold taxes from their Social Security benefit checks, rather than face a potential bill during tax filing season.

    Separately, a temporary senior deduction of up to $6,000 for individuals ages 65 and over may help to indirectly reduce taxes on Social Security benefits.

    Industry observers note that that deduction, part of the One Massive Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, helps reduce retirees' taxable income, according to Steffen. It's in place through 2028. Because the break phases out for individuals with modified adjusted gross income starting at $75,000 — and for married couples with $150,000 — it's vital to watch your income if you're close to those limits, Steffen noted.

    Recent findings suggest that "Keep in mind that if you're over 65, you might qualify for this deduction," Steffen said. "But if you let your income get too big, you might lose the deduction.".

    Moreover, any extra income that causes you to lose the deduction may also come with its own taxes, making it more expensive, according to Steffen.

    "What we've been telling our clients is that tax planning is a lot more complicated than it used to be, and you can't do it on the back of an envelope anymore," he said. "You need to use good tools that can do good calculations for you.".

    Individuals who claim Social Security retirement benefits before their full retirement age and who continue to work may be subject to withholdings.

    Industry observers note that in 2027, individuals under full retirement age may earn up to $25,560 per year, up from $24,480 in 2026, without adjustments to their Social Security benefits. For every $2 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits will be withheld.

    Importantly, those withholdings are not lost completely. Once a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, the withheld money will be credited to their benefits over their remaining lifespan.

    In the year individuals reach full retirement age, the retirement earnings test limit is higher — $67,920 per year in 2027, up from $65,160 per year in 2026. For every $3 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits is withheld.

    Starting the month a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, no earnings are withheld.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Jacksonville Jaguars entered Sunday at 7-2 having emerged as a Super Bowl favorite out of the AFC.

    The New York Giants doused them with a splash of cold water.

    Plagued by red-zone woes, officiating controversy and a questionable late-game decision by Jacksonville head coach Liam Coen, the Jaguars fell 23-18 to the Giants.

    Jacksonville had a shot to tie the game with fourth-and-goal at the Fresh York 8-yard line and 3:40 remaining on the clock. New York led 23-15, and the Jaguars were down to one timeout.

    But instead of going for a potential game-tying touchdown and 2-point conversion, Coen opted to kick a field goal that cut the deficit to five points, apparently betting on the Jaguars' defense to get them the ball back.

    Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars suffered a stunning loss to the Giants on Sunday.

    Sources indicate that they did not. Cam Skattebo ran for a first down before the two-minute warning with the Jaguars having exhausted their final timeout. The Giants were able to kneel out the remaining two minutes of game clock in victory formation.

    According to recent reports, it added up to a jarring loss for the now 7-3 Jaguars on the heels of an aggressive trade deadline in which they made several big swings to bolster their hopes of a Super Bowl run. The Giants, meanwhile, improved to 6-3-1 to maintain their lead in the NFC East over the 5-6 Dallas Cowboys.

    In a recent development, coen was asked about his decision to kick the late field goal in his postgame news conference. He cited analytics charts and described going for a touchdown as a "hope play.".

    According to recent reports, "We talked about it a few times," Coen said. "Our defense, they hadn't done anything up until that point. Everything about the charts and everything talked about it said kick the field goal, get within five points.

    In a recent development, "Go get a stop, and you feel pretty good about where you're at. Just executing that down-and-distance on a fourth down is kinda challenging. Especially, they're zero blitzing you every play, the ball's gonna come out. It's like a hope play.".

    Coen's comments Sunday stood in contrast to a previous discussion with Barstool Sports about a strikingly similar, but not identical hypothetical scenario.

    In that discussion, Coen was asked about whether to kick a field goal or go for it when down by eight points at the 8-yard line with one key caveat: "When you're up against the greatest quarterback of all time.".

    Industry observers note that "You've gotta go for it," Coen mentioned. … "It's weird down there — and you're in an opportunity to score a touchdown, you're that close. We all know how hard it is to score in the red zone in this league. … I think you've gotta be aggressive there.".

    Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy is certainly not "the greatest quarterback of all time." It's not clear if Coen would have made a different decision if facing a different caliber of quarterback.

    According to recent reports, the Giants were in control virtually from the start. They took a 10-3 advantage into the second quarter and a 20-6 lead into halftime. While McCarthy kept Newly introduced York's offense moving and scoring, the Jaguars repeatedly broke down in the red zone.

    Jacksonville's first three trips to the red zone produced 6 points courtesy of two field goals and a turnover on downs in the third quarter when a fourth-and-1 pass from Trevor Lawrence fell incomplete.

    Jacksonville's fourth red-zone trip produced controversy on a third-down effort to cut their deficit to one possession.

    They appeared to do just that when Parker Washington made a leaping catch in the back of the end zone and got both feet in bounds. But officials ruled that he didn't maintain control of the ball as he hit the ground.

    Coen used Jacksonville's last remaining challenge to challenge the call on the field. The ball moved in Washington's hands after Washington hit the ground, but he never appeared to lose control of it.

    But officials didn't see enough to overturn the call on the field, and the ruling of an incomplete pass stood. The result was a fourth down in which the Jaguars settled for a field goal to cut their deficit to 20-9.

    Jacksonville finally cracked the end zone with a touchdown pass from Lawrence to Brian Thomas Jr. with 6:39 remaining. A failed 2-point conversion left the Jaguars facing a 23-15 hole.

    Then came the decision that will prompt plenty of questions for Coen.

    In the end, the Jaguars woke up on offense and limited the Giants on defense as they outgained New York, 354 yards to 238. Lawrence completed 25 of 47 passes for 301 yards with 1 touchdown and 2 interceptions.

    McCarthy completed 18 of 38 passes for 173 yards with 1 touchdown. But he didn't turn the ball over as the Giants won the takeaway battle, 2 to 1.

    The result will leave the Jaguars with plenty to ponder ahead of a Week 12 home game against the Titans.

    The Giants do indeed have the ability to run the clock out.

    The discussion for this game will be Jacksonville focused. First it will be whether or not Parker Washington deserved a touchdown on his reception in the end zone that was ruled incomplete.

    The second will be Liam Coen's decision to be on the 8-yard line facing fourth down and opting to kick a meaningless field goal rather than trying to tie the game.

    Giants running back Cam Skattebo noted that he was retiring the backflip after what happened to Aidan Hutchinson tearing his ACL celebrating a sack.

    Skattebo picked up the first down at the two-minute warning. Jacksonville has no timeouts left, so this should be the ball game.

    The Giants running back celebrated the only way he knew how: with a backflip.

    The Giants are in the driver's seat needing a few first downs to seal with win against the Jaguars.

    Sources indicate that on second and seven, JJ McCarthy hit rookie wideout Malachi Fields for the 19-yard gain. Jacksonville only has one timeout left.

    Recent findings suggest that the Jaguars were grooving down the field, but the offense stalled in the red zone. After several incompletions by Trevor Lawrence to the end zone, Jacksonville opted to kick the field goal.

    Sources indicate that cam Little connected on the 26-yard field goal. Jacksonville now trails 23-18 with 3:40 left.

    Recent findings suggest that after an incompletion on first down, JJ McCarthy hit Malik Nabers for an eight-yard gain. An offensive lineman was then whistled for unnecessary roughness for hitting a Jaguars defender late.

    After another incompletion, Latest York was forced to punt.

    Jacksonville gets the ball back down 8 with 5:47 left to go in regulation.

    It looked like it was going to be a broken play as Trevor Lawrence had time, but couldn't find anybody.

    All of a sudden he fired it to the end zone and Brian Thomas Jr. had gotten wide open.

    Jacksonville decided to go for two. He floated it into the end zone but it was picked, which doesn't mean much for the stat sheet other than the attempt failed.

    Upcoming York leads 23-15 with 6:39 left to go.

    Giants rookie kicker Dominic Zvada had made a 53-yard field goal and missed a 32-yarder.

    Zvada lined up for a 43-yard attempt and drilled it.

    Upcoming York leads 23-9 with 10 minutes to go.

    Trevor Lawrence's tough day continues.

    He had an incompletion on first down, and then threw his second interception of the game.

    The officials in this game are certainly apparent.

    Latest York picked up seven yards on first down, but it was called back due to offensive holding.

    JJ McCarthy then had three consecutive incompletions. Newly introduced York took 1:02 off the clock and punted back to Jacksonville.

    The Giants lead 20-9 with 11:15 left in the game.

    It looked like Parker Washington made his latest video game-esque catch, but it was ruled an incompletion.

    Industry observers note that replay on the broadcast had JJ Watt swearing that it was a touchdown. Even the rules analyst on the broadcast remarked it should have been a touchdown. Jacksonville challenged the play and the ruling was upheld.

    While the Jaguars didn't get a touchdown out of it, Jacksonville did add three with a field goal.

    Newly introduced York leads 20-9 with 12:17 left in the game.

    New York's drive consisted of two incompletions and then JJ McCarthy scrambling for a massive 29-yard gain.

    It was erased by a holding call.

    On third and 16 McCarthy had his third incompletion of the drive and Latest York was forced to punt.

    Jacksonville takes over trailing 20-6 at the start of the fourth quarter.

    Jacksonville got down to the 11-yard line. Trailing 20-6 with a minute to go in the third quarter, Liam Coen opted to go for it.

    Trevor Lawrence stared down his target and tried to thread the needle to Jakobi Meyers, but the Giants defense was all over it for the turnover on downs.

    Industry observers note that the Jaguars defense had been on the field for over five minutes. Jacksonville needing something and it came in the form of a Cam Skattebo fumble.

    Jacksonville scooped it, and the defender spun away from the line and took it back 42 yards to give the Jaguars great field position.

    Recent findings suggest that jacksonville couldn't capitalize on Fresh York's missed field goal. Trevor Lawrence had two incompletions sandwiching a one-yard gain by Bhayshul Tuten.

    Upcoming York leads 20-6 with 9 minutes to go in the third quarter.

    It has been revealed that rookie kicker Dominic Zvada had made a 53-yard field goal already in the game. It looked like his 32-yard attempt was going to be easy, but he planted weird and ended up pushing it wide left.

    Giants head coach John Harbaugh is showing he trusts his rookie kicker.

    Dominic Zvada has been inconsistent this season, but nailed a 54-yarder toward the end of the first half to put the Giants up 20-6.

    Trevor Lawrence put on a magic show in the backfield. He eluded three different sets of pressure from the Giants and managed to get a pass off.

    Brenton Strange caught it even though it wasn't nearly enough for the first down, it was still impressive. It ended up being just a gain of four.

    After the two-minute warning, Jacksonville punted trailing 17-6.

    According to recent reports, this might be Abdul Carter's breakout game. He has found a mismatch on the Jaguars' offensive line because he is consistently going after Trevor Lawrence in the backfield.

    Carter already has two sacks in the game and four tackles overall.

    New York drove the field against the Jacksonville defense.

    The Giants' nine-play, 66-yard touchdown drive ends with JJ McCarthy finding Malik Nabers in the back of the end zone as the wide receiver just manages to get his two touches in.

    Jacksonville's offensive drive stalled in the red zone. The drive was highlighted by a nice 21-yard grab by Parker Washington.

    On third and 12, Trevor Lawrence fumbled the snap, but was able to recover it. He couldn't find anything downfield and took off. He only picked up 8 yards.

    Cam Little came on and nailed the 35-yard field goal to decrease the Giants' lead to four points.

    New York leads 10-6 early in the second quarter.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump suggested Saturday that there could be a bright spot in the latest incursion into the FBI computer database.

    The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information.

    The hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center (NCIC), a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW. The database is restricted to law enforcement use but not classified and it is unclear what data was extracted.

    CNN had first reported on the suspected hack, citing sources familiar with the issue.

    In a wide-ranging interview on Fox, Trump said there could be upside from the news.

    "Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," he remarked. "I always like to put things on a positive spin.".

    Sources indicate that this would be the second recent intrusion into the FBI system; the previous one came in September, when a group known as "ShinyHunters" broke into an FBI jobs website. The result compromised data on current and former FBI employees and shut down part of the agency's operations until the issue was resolved.

    Trump mentioned it's possible there could be information gleaned from the latest hack.

    Industry observers note that "I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?" he said. "People should hear about it, because it actually put our country in danger, and so maybe we'll learn things that we wouldn't have learned otherwise.".

    The FBI did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
    • Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
    • The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

    Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

    The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

    The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

    Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

    Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

    After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

    They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

    Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

    We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

    It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

    As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

    On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

    Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

    If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

    The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance.".

    The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

    Industry observers note that barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks upcoming CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

    In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to swiftly disclose any sales.

    Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

    That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

    Industry observers note that the case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

    Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

    According to recent reports, in the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

    All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

    In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway states it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

    Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

    It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

    In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

    Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

    Recent findings suggest that WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

    You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

    Two of the — well, all of the vital ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

    One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

    And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

    And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds.".

    Berkshire market capitalization: $1,259,897,054,755.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.
    • Mount has had a torrid time with injuries since signing from Chelsea in a £55m-deal three years ago, starting only 25 Premier League games for United in that time.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.

    Mount has had a torrid time with injuries since signing from Chelsea in a £55m-deal three years ago, starting only 25 Premier League games for United in that time.

    The 27-year-old has been successfully deployed by Carrick in a central midfield role during pre-season, leading to speculation that United may not make another expected signing in that department.

    But Mount played only 18 minutes of Saturday’s 1-1 draw against the European champions in Gothenburg before being replaced by Scotland international Tyler Fletcher.

    “He [Mount] got kicked. We just wanted to be careful and look after him,” Carrick, the United head coach, told reporters in Sweden.

    “We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful.”.

    Post-match video footage indicated Mount walking freely on to the United bus without the aid of a protective boot or knee support.

    #73475. 26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1921 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money.
    • At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage.
    • For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money.

    At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage.

    For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states.

    He does it by living with roommates in Washington, D.C., walking or biking instead of driving, eating free meals at work and rarely spending beyond his basic needs. Even when he splurges on something fun, he keeps things modest; in August, that meant a baseball game and a single $7 beer.

    "I guess something else that probably does make me a little bit unique is I really don't feel joy when I buy things," he indicates. "I feel like I have what I need.".

    There is a goal behind all that saving. Broomfield has pursued financial independence since college and now expects to reach his target of $750,000 in investments within the next year, well ahead of his original goal of doing so by age 30. As his income has climbed, his lifestyle has largely stayed the same, he indicates.

    Here's how Broomfield keeps his spending so low and what he looks to do once he no longer needs the paycheck.

    Broomfield grew up in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the son of two military veterans. He and his siblings had to set aside half of everything they earned growing up. They could spend the other half or earn interest from their parents by putting that money away, too.

    By his teenage years, Broomfield had become a disciplined saver. At the time, he dreamed of using his cash stash to buy some of the familiar trappings of wealth.

    Industry observers note that "I wanted a Lamborghini and I wanted some nice penthouse," he says. "I just wanted them because I thought other people wanted them.".

    In a recent development, at 17, Broomfield discovered Mr. Money Mustache, a personal finance blog by a former software engineer who retired at 30. The blog advocates living frugally and investing much of your income to build a portfolio large enough to support you through withdrawals, without needing a paycheck. It introduced Broomfield to the financial independence, retire early — or FIRE — movement and gave all that saving a newly introduced purpose.

    "All I had to do was live super frugally and I could actually reach financial freedom by the time I was 30 and go do whatever actually made me happy in life," he states.

    The idea stuck with him. After graduating from Knox College in 2022, Broomfield moved to Northern Virginia for a job paying more than $100,000 a year and set a goal of reaching $750,000 in investments before 30 while spending less than $25,000 a year.

    He also decided to start at $0. Broomfield had roughly $50,000 in savings when he graduated, with his parents having covered the portion of his college tuition not paid for by scholarships. He wanted his FIRE total to reflect only what he earned after college.

    In his first year after college, Broomfield was "super geeked out" about reaching financial freedom, he says.

    "It's almost the only thing I thought about, because I was building all these new habits and making real money for really the first time in my life," he notes.

    That enthusiasm sometimes took him to extremes. He even considered living in a van parked in his employer's garage to avoid paying rent.

    "I crunched the numbers on it, and effectively every year that I spent living in a van rather than paying rent would allow me to retire approximately one month faster," he indicates. "It just [didn't] seem really worth it to go to that extreme.".

    But Broomfield still found satisfaction in squeezing every dollar out of his budget. He once biked two miles to a grocery store to save $1 on toothpaste rather than buy it at the Whole Foods next to his apartment.

    Sources indicate that "For a lot of people, they feel their wins by buying stuff for themselves," Broomfield indicates. "I get my wins by seeing how much I can invest.".

    Looking back, Broomfield acknowledges that some of his early efforts to save money made little difference in how rapidly he could reach financial independence.

    "I never expect anybody else to do exactly what I'm doing," he indicates. "I know I'm way more of a geek about this than most people, and I'm particularly well positioned to be able to live this kind of life.".

    Broomfield's core living expenses totaled $1,477 in August, excluding savings, investments and payments toward his graduate school tuition.

    Here's a breakdown of where his money went that month, including those additional payments:.

    Roughly 90% of Broomfield's income went to savings and investments in August, a fairly typical month for him, he says. He put about $7,931 into his 401(k) and another $10,000 into a taxable brokerage account.

    Another $700 went toward a 0% interest employer tuition repayment initiative with a former employer, leaving him with a remaining balance of $16,800 in August.

    Housing is Broomfield's biggest expense, though he keeps costs down by sharing an apartment with four roommates. In a neighborhood where one-bedroom apartments commonly rent for more than $2,000, the arrangement saves him about $1,000 a month.

    It has been revealed that one thing Broomfield is willing to splurge on is a martial arts gym membership. He pays $229 a month to train as a kickboxer, even though he could work out for free at Google's office gym. Broomfield considers it a "young person's sport" and doesn't want to postpone competing until after he reaches financial independence. It's also a way to socialize with other amateur fighters who share his interest.

    Broomfield doesn't own a car and generally walks, bikes or takes public transportation. Google covers his daily Metro commute, which helps keep his transportation costs low. He tries to meet friends near Metro stations and, when visiting his grandfather in Virginia, takes public transit as far as he can before using Uber for the last leg of the trip.

    Before joining Google, Broomfield typically spent around $200 a month on food. Now that he eats most of his meals at work, he spends about $70 a month on average. His $28 food bill in August was especially low because he had ingredients left over from July.

    He also cooks less at home these days. Previously, he relied more on batch cooking, including pressure cooker chili that makes nine servings for about $2 each. For snacks, he might have a bowl of Raisin Bran or celery with peanut butter.

    “I did the math once, and peanut butter was the lowest cost thing per gram of protein in the entire grocery store,” he says in a video on his YouTube channel, which he started in 2023 to document his FIRE journey.

    For entertainment, he relies on the free version of YouTube, where he watches educational content about startups, business and entrepreneurship, or listens to music.

    Broomfield expects to make about $323,000 in 2026, more than triple the roughly $100,000 he earned in his first year out of college. His compensation rose to about $120,000 over his first three years, then jumped to $200,000 when he joined Amazon Web Services in 2025. After a brief stint at Capital One, he moved to Google this year. By keeping his expenses low, investing most of what he earns and riding an upward-trending stock market, he has built up about $650,000 in investments since graduating from college.

    Broomfield earns money from his YouTube channel as well, which has expanded to offer personal finance and career advice. About $48,000 of his projected income this year will come from the channel and a related career-coaching business.

    Even as his income has grown, Broomfield has stuck with roommates, public transportation and the same modest spending habits.

    In a recent development, "I've really separated how happy I am from how much money I spend," he says. "I truly don't believe that I would be significantly happier if I spent a lot more money.".

    According to recent reports, much of the money he doesn't spend goes straight into investments. He maxes out tax-advantaged accounts including his 401(k) and HSA, and has sometimes contributed 100% of his paycheck to his 401(k) early in the year to reach the annual limit as promptly as possible.

    Broomfield keeps his investment strategy simple, favoring broad-market index funds.

    It has been revealed that "I don't try and pick individual stocks. I just don't have the time to do the research and understand the risk and potential returns of those individual stocks," he states. "And the research indicates that most people who try to pick individual stocks don't end up doing better than if they just invested in the stock market as a whole.".

    He avoids cryptocurrency for a similar reason. Broomfield notes he doesn't understand what gives it value and doesn't want to put money into investments he doesn't understand.

    At his current pace, Broomfield expects to reach his $750,000 investment goal within the next year.

    When Broomfield discovered the FIRE movement at 17, he worried about being stuck in what he imagined as a "soul-crushing" 9-to-5 office job until age 65. He saw financial independence as a way to quit working altogether.

    But while financial independence would give him enough money to live without a paycheck, Broomfield no longer sees early retirement as the goal.

    “Once I reach financial freedom, maybe this is a little ironic, but I actually think I will keep working,” he claims.

    Sources indicate that his YouTube business already earns enough in most months to cover his expenses without a full-time job. With that income and his growing investments, Broomfield hopes to eventually build a business of his own, potentially in AI security.

    "Having complete ownership and complete buy-in to something that's my own. That sounds really exciting to me," he claims.

    According to recent reports, whatever he chooses to do, Broomfield sees financial independence as a way to keep his options open. He bases his savings goal on the so-called “4% rule, a retirement guideline that suggests withdrawing 4% of your investments in the first year, then adjusting withdrawals for inflation.

    For Broomfield, that would mean roughly $30,000 a year from a $750,000 portfolio. That's enough to cover his current expenses, though he recognizes that could change if he eventually starts a family.

    It has been revealed that "There's a very good chance I won't want to live the way I do forever. That's one of the reasons I'm doing it now. I'm young. I'm healthy. I'm single," he states. "I totally understand that somebody with a family probably doesn't want to live with a bunch of roommates.".

    But the money Broomfield has already saved gives him more freedom to choose where and how much he works without feeling tied to a paycheck.

    "Having that peace of mind to know that I'll be fine, even if I can't find work promptly or even if I get laid off tomorrow, that has just been a huge breath of fresh air for myself," he claims.

    Quantum computing’s first real-world payoff may come in energy, not drug discovery

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, for years, the case for quantum computing has rested on ambitious promises, from discovering fresh drugs by simulating how molecules behave to optimizing supply chains and airline schedules.
    • But quantum software, which uses algorithms designed to solve complex problems faster than conventional computers, is already being tested on a more immediate challenge: the energy transition, from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production.
    • Phasecraft, a quantum software tech giant founded in Bristol, England, in 2019, is one of the firms putting the technology to work in energy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, for years, the case for quantum computing has rested on ambitious promises, from discovering fresh drugs by simulating how molecules behave to optimizing supply chains and airline schedules. Many of the biggest aims are still likely to be years, if not decades, away.

    But quantum software, which uses algorithms designed to solve complex problems faster than conventional computers, is already being tested on a more immediate challenge: the energy transition, from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production.

    Phasecraft, a quantum software tech giant founded in Bristol, England, in 2019, is one of the firms putting the technology to work in energy. It raised $34 million in Series B funding in 2025, and in September this year announced looks to set up U.S. headquarters in Arlington, Virginia.

    There are enormous opportunities to solve problems that are both vital for energy security and commercially valuable, Ashley Montanaro, co-founder and CEO of Phasecraft, told CNBC.

    Phasecraft isn't alone in applying quantum software to the energy industry.

    Sources indicate that quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture.

    Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently.

    In a separate project, ORCA worked with Japanese software company JIJ on a challenge power companies face: deciding which generators to switch on or off, and when, to meet demand at the lowest cost.

    That project also involved BP and the National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC), the U.K.'s national laboratory for quantum computing, which is part of the government-backed U.K. Research and Innovation. The involvement of the NQCC, like that of ARPA-E, suggests governments are paying close attention to quantum software's potential role in energy, as are companies such as BP.

    Sources indicate that for Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator (NESO), the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The manufacturer notes its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing.

    Phasecraft believes its grid software could be particularly sought after in Asia, where electrification is rapidly expanding, increasing the need for grid resilience to balance high and growing demand with the intermittent supply offered by renewables.

    According to recent reports, the manufacturer is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones.

    It has been revealed that separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen.

    Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, Montanaro mentioned the returns were there too.

    "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he noted.

    Who notes you can't tailgate an IPO?Traders are preparing for this week's blockbuster Anthropic IPO in different ways, including buying options on one publicly-traded fund that invests in private assets.The Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ) is a publicly-traded, closed-end fund that invests in equity, equity-linked instruments, or shares of private funds and venture companies to gain exposure to private companies. Right now, 14% of the fund's assets are tied to Anthropic, according to the firm's website.Options volume on the fund jumped to more than 10x the 30-day average Monday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Of the 42,300 contracts traded by midday, 41,800 were calls, with just 141 puts likely opened by buyers.

    Sources indicate that just shy of $5.5 million in options premium on DXYZ traded on Monday, with almost all of it tied to calls, but just marginally more spent buying than selling calls, according to SpotGamma. The highest-volume contract is currently the 30-strike call expiring Friday, a 90-cent contract that needs the fund to rally 19% into the weekend to pay off.Traders may want to be wary of how the fund traded around the SpaceX IPO: DXYZ surged almost 150% in May before unwinding all the gains in the weeks ahead of SpaceX's debut. Since then, the fund has barely moved, trading around $26.There are other bullish signs surrounding Anthropic's IPO in the derivatives markets. Current prices for perpetual futures on the blockchain exchange Hyperliquid are implying an opening price of $98, a big pop from the $70-$78 price range quoted in the tech giant's amended S1 filing. The AI giant is expected to price Wednesday evening and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.
